claim: Self-propagating CRISPR-based gene drive systems are likely to be highly invasive in wild populations despite drive-resistant alleles.
source: Recent reports have suggested that self-propagating CRISPR-based gene drive systems are unlikely to efficiently invade wild populations due to drive-resistant alleles that prevent cutting. Here we develop mathematical models based on existing empirical data to explicitly test this assumption for population alteration drives. Our models show that although resistance prevents spread to fixation in large populations, even the least effective drive systems reported to date are likely to be highly invasive.
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical models developed by the authors based on existing empirical data, as stated in the abstract.

claim: Releasing a small number of organisms with gene drive will often cause invasion of the local population.
source: Releasing a small number of organisms will often cause invasion of the local population, followed by invasion of additional populations connected by very low rates of gene flow.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical models and simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gene drive can invade additional populations connected by very low rates of gene flow.
source: Releasing a small number of organisms will often cause invasion of the local population, followed by invasion of additional populations connected by very low rates of gene flow.
evidence: This is demonstrated through structured population models showing escape probabilities across connected subpopulations.

claim: Initiating contained field trials could potentially result in unintended spread to additional populations.
source: Hence, initiating contained field trials as tentatively endorsed by the National Academies report on gene drive could potentially result in unintended spread to additional populations.
evidence: This inference is drawn from the modeling results showing high invasiveness even with small releases.

claim: Self-propagating gene drive is best suited to applications that seek to affect all wild populations of the target species.
source: Our mathematical results suggest that self-propagating gene drive is best suited to applications such as malaria prevention that seek to affect all wild populations of the target species.
evidence: This recommendation is based on the inference from modeling results showing difficulty in containing gene drives.

claim: CRISPR-based gene drive systems can bias inheritance of desired traits by cutting a wild-type allele and copying the drive system in its place.
source: CRISPR-based gene drive systems can bias inheritance of desired traits by cutting a wild-type allele and copying the drive system in its place (Esvelt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by Esvelt et al., 2014.

claim: Successful CRISPR gene drive systems have been reported in yeast and fruit flies.
source: Following reports of successful CRISPR gene drive systems in yeast (DiCarlo et al., 2015) and fruit flies (Gantz and Bier, 2015), scientists emphasized the need to employ strategies beyond traditional barrier containment as a laboratory safeguard (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2016; Akbari et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies in yeast and fruit flies.

claim: Drive resistance can result from mutations that block cutting by the CRISPR nuclease.
source: Drive resistance can result from mutations that block cutting by the CRISPR nuclease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR gene drive mechanisms.

claim: Resistance is predicted to prevent drive fixation in wild populations unless additional mitigating strategies are employed.
source: Resistance can arise from standing genetic variation at the drive locus or because the drive mechanism is not perfectly efficient and is predicted to prevent drive fixation in wild populations unless additional mitigating strategies are employed (Burt, 2003; Deredec et al., 2008; Esvelt et al., 2014; Noble et al., 2017; Marshall et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical and modeling work.

claim: An allele can spread to significant frequency without fixing.
source: While we agree that resistance should prevent drive fixation, an allele can nonetheless spread to significant frequency without fixing.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about population genetics dynamics.

claim: CRISPR-based gene drive systems function by converting drive-heterozygotes into homozygotes in the late germline or early embryo.
source: CRISPR-based gene drive systems function by converting drive-heterozygotes into homozygotes in the late germline or early embryo (Esvelt et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A CRISPR nuclease encoded in the drive construct cuts at the corresponding wild-type allele producing a double-strand break.
source: First, a CRISPR nuclease encoded in the drive construct cuts at the corresponding wild-type allele—its target prescribed by an independently expressed guide RNA (gRNA)—producing a double-strand break (Jinek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: Double-strand breaks can be repaired through homology-directed repair, producing a second copy of the gene drive construct.
source: This break is then repaired either through homology-directed repair, producing a second copy of the gene drive construct, or through a nonhomologous repair pathway (non-homologous end joining, NHEJ, or microhomology-mediated end joining, MMEJ), which typically introduces a mutation at the target site (Mali et al., 2013; Cong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Nonhomologous repair pathways typically introduce a mutation at the target site.
source: This break is then repaired either through homology-directed repair, producing a second copy of the gene drive construct, or through a nonhomologous repair pathway (non-homologous end joining, NHEJ, or microhomology-mediated end joining, MMEJ), which typically introduces a mutation at the target site (Mali et al., 2013; Cong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Mutations from nonhomologous repair generally result in resistance to future cutting by the gene drive.
source: Because the drive target is determined through sequence homology, such a mutation generally results in resistance to future cutting by the gene drive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of CRISPR targeting through sequence homology.

claim: Drive-resistant alleles are expected to exist in wild populations due to standing genetic variation.
source: Moreover, drive-resistant alleles are expected to exist in wild populations simply due to standing genetic variation (Unckless et al., 2017; Drury et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on standing genetic variation.

claim: The homing efficiencies of reported drive systems typically range from 0.37 to 0.99.
source: Given that the homing efficiencies of reported drive systems typically range from 0.37 to 0.99 (Appendix 1—table 1), current drive systems can clearly invade in deterministic models.
evidence: This is supported by empirical data compiled in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: Current drive systems can invade in deterministic models.
source: Given that the homing efficiencies of reported drive systems typically range from 0.37 to 0.99 (Appendix 1—table 1), current drive systems can clearly invade in deterministic models.
evidence: This is an inference based on the empirical homing efficiency data and the invasion condition.

claim: In finite populations, the fate of initially rare alleles is determined by both selection and stochastic fluctuations.
source: However, in finite populations, the fate of initially rare alleles is determined not only by selection but also by stochastic fluctuations (Wright, 1931; Fisher, 1930; Haldane, 1927).
evidence: This is established knowledge in population genetics, supported by classic citations.

claim: Stochastic models are required to predict the probability that a drive will invade a population upon introduction of a very small number of individuals.
source: Therefore, stochastic models are required to predict the probability that a drive will invade a population upon the introduction of a very small number of individuals, even when deterministic models predict that they are to invade.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of deterministic models for small populations.

claim: Homing-based drives were among the likeliest to invade of various drive alternatives according to a previous stochastic model.
source: A previous, and arguably prescient, stochastic model of endonuclease drive containment found that homing-based drives, such as those subsequently developed using CRISPR, were among the likeliest to invade of the various drive alternatives (Marshall, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior modeling study.

claim: Assuming neutral resistance represents the worst-case scenario for drive spread.
source: This ordering of the parameters conservatively represents the worst-case scenario for drive spread (Comparison with deterministic model).
evidence: This is stated as a modeling assumption with reference to supporting analysis.

claim: For conservative drive efficiency (P=0.5), the drive on average irreversibly alters a majority of the population.
source: In all three cases, the drive, on average, irreversibly alters a majority of the population, either via invasion of the drive itself or via spread of drive-created resistant alleles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Peak drive distributions are bimodal, with one mode centered around the initial frequency and one centered around maximum values.
source: We find that these distributions are bimodal, with one mode centered around the initial frequency (corresponding to drift leading rapidly to extinction) and one centered roughly around the maximum values observed in the large-release scenarios in Figure 1D.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: If the migration rate is extremely low, the drive is effectively contained in the initial subpopulation.
source: Our results in Figure 2 suggest that if the migration rate is extremely low, then the drive is effectively contained in the initial subpopulation.
evidence: This is shown by the structured population model results in Figure 2.

claim: If the migration rate is high, the drive is almost guaranteed to invade all subpopulations linked to the originating one.
source: If the migration rate is high, the drive is almost guaranteed to invade all subpopulations linked to the originating one.
evidence: This is shown by the structured population model results in Figure 2.

claim: Peak drive can be substantially increased by associating a fitness cost with resistance.
source: Moreover, in line with previous deterministic results, we find that peak drive can be substantially increased by associating a fitness cost with resistance (Figure 8), which could be expected for drive constructs intended for large-scale application, utilizing methods such as multiplex targeting of essential genes (Esvelt et al., 2014; Noble et al., 2017; Marshall et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results in Figure 8 and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: High selfing probabilities are required to reduce peak drive and the probability of invasion for moderate drive costs.
source: We find that even in this scenario, high selfing probabilities are required to reduce peak drive and the probability of invasion for moderate drive costs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the inbreeding model results shown in Figure 9.

claim: The key qualitative finding that peak drive is difficult to reliably contain below a socially tolerable threshold appears robust to a variety of mitigating factors.
source: However, for alteration drives, our key qualitative finding—that peak drive is difficult to reliably contain below a socially tolerable threshold following a very small release of organisms—appears robust to a variety of mitigating factors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the various sensitivity analyses performed in the study.

claim: Current first-generation CRISPR-based gene drive systems for population alteration are capable of far-reaching spread, even for very small releases.
source: Our results suggest that current first-generation CRISPR-based gene drive systems for population alteration are capable of far-reaching—perhaps, for species distributed worldwide, global—spread, even for very small releases.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the modeling and simulation results.

claim: A simple, constitutively expressed CRISPR nuclease and guide RNA cassette targeting the neutral site of insertion may be capable of altering many populations.
source: A simple, constitutively expressed CRISPR nuclease and guide RNA cassette targeting the neutral site of insertion—an arrangement that could occur accidentally—may be capable of altering many populations of the target species depending on the homing efficiency of the organism in question.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results for low-efficiency drives.

claim: Resistance is not a major impediment to invasion of unintended populations.
source: More generally, resistance can be problematic for intentional applications of gene drives, but we find that it is not a major impediment to invasion of unintended populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results showing invasion despite resistance.

claim: Most laboratory gene drive systems are unlikely to cause ecological changes.
source: However, we consider the answer to the second question to be clearer: although most laboratory gene drive systems are unlikely to cause ecological changes—they are typically predicted to be transient and are not designed to alter traits of the host organism, least of all interactions with other species
evidence: This is speculation based on the typical design of laboratory gene drive systems.

claim: Substantial social backlash could be triggered by unauthorized spread of a self-propagating gene drive.
source: the history of genetic engineering offers many examples suggesting that substantial social backlash could be triggered by unauthorized spread of a self-propagating gene drive (Funk and Rainie, 2015; Couzin and Kaiser, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on public perception of genetic engineering.

claim: Unauthorized spread could significantly reduce public support for interventions against diseases such as malaria.
source: Any such event could significantly reduce public support for interventions against diseases such as malaria that could possibly save millions of lives.
evidence: This is speculation about potential social consequences based on historical examples.

claim: The primary factor in determining drive spread between adjacent populations is the average number of migrants per generation.
source: we find that the primary factor in determining drive spread between adjacent populations is the average number of migrants per generation (Analytic formulae for the escape probability in structured populations), which can, in principle, be compared between models.
evidence: This is derived from the analytical formulas developed in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Laboratories in regions with endemic wild populations may wish to refrain from constructing self-propagating systems capable of invading those populations.
source: Given the risk that organisms may escape through accidents or outside intervention, laboratories in regions with endemic wild populations may wish to refrain from constructing self-propagating systems capable of invading those populations and undergoing unwanted spread.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the modeling results showing high invasiveness.

claim: Laboratories in regions with endemic wild populations can reliably prevent accidental invasion by employing intrinsic molecular confinement mechanisms.
source: Laboratories in regions with endemic wild populations can reliably prevent accidental invasion by employing intrinsic molecular confinement mechanisms such as synthetic site targeting or split drive as recommended by the National Academies' report on gene drives (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2016).
evidence: This recommendation is supported by citation to the National Academies report.

claim: There could be a high likelihood of unwanted spread across international borders, even from ostensibly isolated islands.
source: Perhaps most importantly, any development efforts looking ahead toward field trials, a component of the staged testing strategy outlined by the National Academies report, should be aware that there could be a high likelihood of unwanted spread across international borders, even from ostensibly isolated islands.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structured population modeling results.

claim: Female Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes can lay hundreds of eggs per lifetime.
source: For example, female Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes can lay hundreds of eggs per lifetime (Hammond et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: When the migration rate is on the order of the inverse of the drive extinction time, the invasion probability is order 1.
source: Thus, when the migration rate is on the order of the inverse of the drive extinction time, the invasion probability is order 1.
evidence: This is derived from the analytical formulas in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Deterministic models predict whether an allele is favored to increase in frequency when initially rare in a wild population.
source: Deterministic models, which assume an infinite, well-mixed population, predict whether an allele is favored to increase in frequency when initially rare in a wild population.
evidence: This is established knowledge about deterministic population genetics models.
